blocks.content: The previous topic covered why normalization matters in the first place, this topic covers the very first rule in the sequence, first normal form, often written 1NF, which requires every column value to be a single, atomic value rather than a list or set crammed into one cell.

This topic covers exactly what atomic means in this context, a concrete example of a table that violates 1NF, and the standard fix, splitting repeating values out into their own properly related table.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646913413-47315669.png
blocks.alt: Building on why normalization matters, first normal form requires atomic column values

blocks.content: 1. What Atomic Means Here

Atomic means a single, indivisible value, one column, one value, no lists, no sets, no multiple values packed into a single cell separated by commas or any other delimiter, a phone column should hold exactly one phone number, not several.
2. A Concrete Violation
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646915244-868239065.png
blocks.alt: A phone column holding two comma separated numbers violates 1NF

blocks.content: Suppose a customers table has a phone column, and one customer has two phone numbers, storing them as a single value like 555-1010, 555-2020 crammed into one cell violates 1NF, this column is no longer holding one atomic value, it is holding a hidden list.

-- Violates 1NF: multiple values packed into one cell
customer_id | name        | phone
1           | Aisha Khan  | 555-1010, 555-2020

blocks.content: 3. Why This Actually Causes Real Problems
blocks.text: 3. Why This Actually Causes Real Problems

blocks.content: A comma packed phone column cannot be reliably queried, finding every customer with phone number 555-2020 now requires parsing text inside the column rather than a simple, direct comparison, and enforcing anything about individual phone numbers, uniqueness for instance, becomes effectively impossible.

4. The Fix, a Separate Related Table
blocks.text: 4. The Fix, a Separate Related Table

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646918387-652746264.png
blocks.alt: Customer phones move into their own separate table, related back to Customers

blocks.content: The standard fix is splitting the repeating values into their own table, a customer_phones table with one row per phone number, referencing the customer through a foreign key, covered in the earlier Foreign Key topic, this is exactly the one to many relationship shape from the earlier Relationships topic.
The corrected structure
5. Repeating Group Columns Are the Same Problem
blocks.text: 5. Repeating Group Columns Are the Same Problem

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646919936-868759934.png
blocks.alt: phone1, phone2, phone3 columns are compared against a separate row per phone

blocks.content: A subtler version of the same 1NF violation is adding phone1, phone2, phone3 columns directly onto the customers table instead of packing them into one cell, this also violates the spirit of 1NF, it hardcodes a fixed number of phone numbers and still mixes what should be a separate entity, a phone number, directly into the customers table.

blocks.title: Repeating columns are a common but subtle 1NF violation
blocks.content: Numbered columns like phone1, phone2, phone3 feel structurally different from a comma packed cell, but they share the same underlying problem, a variable length list of values forced into a fixed table shape.
6. What a Properly Atomic Table Looks Like
blocks.text: 6. What a Properly Atomic Table Looks Like

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646921551-201595818.png
blocks.alt: Every cell holds exactly one value, with no nested lists or sets inside any cell

blocks.content: A table satisfying 1NF has the property that every cell, in every row, holds exactly one indivisible value, this property is what makes standard SQL operations, filtering, sorting, joining, work correctly and predictably against every column.
7. Before and After, Side by Side
blocks.text: 7. Before and After, Side by Side

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646923079-567090569.png
blocks.alt: Before 1NF used comma separated values, after 1NF each cell holds one value

blocks.content: Comparing the two designs directly, the comma packed version looks more compact at first glance, but the properly split version is the one that actually supports reliable queries, correct constraints, and clean joins, exactly the concerns the rest of this course builds on.
8. Common Mistakes

["Packing multiple values into a single column using a delimiter like a comma or semicolon","Adding numbered repeating columns, phone1, phone2, phone3, instead of a properly related table","Assuming 1NF only applies to text columns, when it applies equally to any column type holding multiple values","Fixing a 1NF violation but forgetting to add the foreign key relating the new table back to the original one"]
items: Packing multiple values into a single column using a delimiter like a comma or semicolon
Adding numbered repeating columns, phone1, phone2, phone3, instead of a properly related table
Assuming 1NF only applies to text columns, when it applies equally to any column type holding multiple values
Fixing a 1NF violation but forgetting to add the foreign key relating the new table back to the original one

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["First normal form requires every column value to be a single, atomic, indivisible value","Comma packed cells and numbered repeating columns are both common violations of the same underlying rule","The fix is always the same, split the repeating values into their own properly related table","The next topic, Second Normal Form, builds on 1NF by addressing columns that depend on only part of a composite key"]
items: First normal form requires every column value to be a single, atomic, indivisible value
Comma packed cells and numbered repeating columns are both common violations of the same underlying rule
The fix is always the same, split the repeating values into their own properly related table
